title: Deployment Guide: Worked Example Weaver (Marimo)
text:
This guide walks you through deploying the Marimo-based Worked Example Weaver to HuggingFace Spaces.



HuggingFace Account: Sign up at huggingface.co
OpenAI API Key: Get one at platform.openai.com





Go to huggingface.co/new-space
Fill in the details:

Space name: worked-example-weaver
License: cc0-1.0 (or your choice)
Select SDK: Docker
Space hardware: CPU basic (free tier)
Visibility: Public (or Private)

Click Create Space




You can either use Git or the web interface to upload files.


# Clone your new Space
git clone https://huggingface.co/spaces/YOUR-USERNAME/worked-example-weaver
cd worked-example-weaver

# Copy files from this directory
cp /path/to/hf-spaces/worked-example-weaver/* .

# Add, commit, and push
git add .
git commit -m "Initial deployment of Worked Example Weaver"
git push




In your Space, click Files → Add file → Upload files
Upload these files:

app.py
Dockerfile
requirements.txt
README.md

Click Commit changes to main






In your Space, go to Settings
Scroll down to Repository secrets
Click New secret
Add your OpenAI API key:

Name: OPENAI_API_KEY
Value: sk-your-actual-key-here

Click Save





Go to the App tab of your Space
HuggingFace will automatically build your Docker container
This takes 5-10 minutes on first deployment
Watch the build logs to see progress




Once the build completes:

The app should automatically load in the iframe
Fill in the learner profile form
Select a concept
Click “Generate My Personalized Example”
Wait 30-60 seconds for the AI to generate your example







Check the build logs in the Logs tab
Ensure all files are present (app.py, Dockerfile, requirements.txt)
Verify Python dependencies are correct





Check that your OPENAI_API_KEY is set correctly in Settings
Verify the key is valid at platform.openai.com/api-keys
Check the logs for specific error messages





Free tier CPU can be slow for AI generation (30-60 seconds is normal)
Consider upgrading to CPU upgrade or T4 GPU for faster generation
Paid tiers available in Space Settings





Make sure you filled in ALL profile fields (name, domain, interest, hobby, goal, level)
Make sure you selected a concept from the dropdown
The button only appears when profile is complete AND a concept is selected







In app.py, line 248:
example_generator = Agent(
    'openai:gpt-5.1',  # Change to 'openai:gpt-4o' or other model
    result_type=PersonalizedWorkedExample,
    ...
)



In app.py, around line 132, add to the CONCEPTS dictionary:
"programming": [
    {
        "name": "Your New Concept",
        "abstract": "Brief description",
        "difficulty": "beginner",
        "typical_use": "When to use it"
    },
    # ... existing concepts
]



In app.py, around line 250, edit the system_prompt parameter to change how the AI generates examples.




After making changes:
git add .
git commit -m "Describe your changes"
git push
HuggingFace will automatically rebuild and redeploy.




HuggingFace Space: Free tier available (CPU basic)
OpenAI API: Pay per use

GPT-5.1: ~$0.02-0.05 per example generated
GPT-4o: ~$0.01-0.02 per example generated
Set usage limits at platform.openai.com

title: Cognitive Load Theory & Educational AI
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this workshop, you will understand:

Cognitive Load Theory: How working memory limits affect learning
The Worked Example Effect: Why studying solutions helps novices
The Personalisation Effect: How familiar contexts reduce cognitive load
How AI can scale these principles in education

title: Cognitive Load Theory & Educational AI
text:
Two Memory Systems


Working Memory
Limited capacity (approximately 4 items)
Volatile (information decays quickly)
Bottleneck for learning

Long-Term Memory
Unlimited capacity
Permanent storage via schemas
Automatic access without effort




The Challenge: Get information from working memory into long-term memory without overload

title: Cognitive Load Theory & Educational AI
text:
Three Types of Cognitive Load









Type
Description
Effect on Learning
Example




Intrinsic
Complexity inherent to the material
Necessary for learning
Learning calculus is inherently complex


Extraneous
Load from poor design or irrelevant info
Hinders learning
Confusing layouts, unfamiliar contexts


Germane
Effort directed at learning
Helps learning
Studying patterns, making connections






Goal: Minimize extraneous load, manage intrinsic load, maximize germane load

title: Cognitive Load Theory & Educational AI
text:
What the Research Shows

“Novice learners who are given worked examples to study perform better on subsequent tests than learners who are required to solve the equivalent problems themselves.”
— NSW Centre for Education Statistics and Evaluation (2017)

Evidence:

Effect size: 0.52 (medium to large)
Strongest for novices
Diminishes as expertise grows
Works across domains (math, programming, science)

title: Cognitive Load Theory & Educational AI
text:
Why It Works


Problem Solving
High cognitive load:

Search for solution
Test approaches
Monitor progress
Learn concept

Little capacity left for learning

Worked Examples
Lower cognitive load:

Solution provided
Focus on understanding
See patterns clearly
Build schemas efficiently

More capacity for learning

title: Cognitive Load Theory & Educational AI
text:
Generic vs. Personalised Examples


Generic
Calculate the correlation
between Variable X and Y.

X: [10, 15, 20, 25, 30]
Y: [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
Higher extraneous load:

Abstract variables
No connection to prior knowledge
No personal relevance


Personalised
You love cycling. Calculate
correlation between training
hours and speed:

Hours: [10, 15, 20, 25, 30]
Speed: [25, 27, 29, 31, 33]
Lower extraneous load:

Familiar context
Connects to existing knowledge
Personally relevant

title: Cognitive Load Theory & Educational AI
text:
Why Personalisation Works

“Familiar contexts require less cognitive effort to process, reducing extraneous cognitive load.”
— Cordova & Lepper (1996)

Benefits:

Reduces extraneous cognitive load
Increases motivation and engagement
Better learning outcomes
Particularly effective with worked examples

title: Cognitive Load Theory & Educational AI
text:
The Challenge of Personalisation
Creating personalised worked examples manually:

30 students × 10 concepts = 300 unique examples
15 minutes per example = 75 hours
Impossible to do at scale

title: Cognitive Load Theory & Educational AI
text:
The AI Solution
AI can generate personalised worked examples:

Create unique examples on demand
Incorporate personal contexts naturally
Maintain quality with structured outputs
Scale to unlimited students




Today’s Goal: Build a tool that generates personalised worked examples using PydanticAI

title: Theory: A CLT-Grounded Diagnostic Taxonomy
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this section, you will:

Recognise the three classical CLT load types and the cognitive architecture they describe
Identify five diagnostic signals visible in student work, derived from CLT plus schema-acquisition research
Match each diagnostic signal to a corresponding intervention strategy
Justify why a fixed diagnostic taxonomy is itself an act of pedagogical decomposition

title: Theory: A CLT-Grounded Diagnostic Taxonomy
section: Where this picks up from the intermediate workshop
text:
Where this picks up from the intermediate workshop
The intermediate workshop established two distinctions:

Cognitive offloading: a tool reduces working-memory load while the student continues to think
Cognitive outsourcing: a tool eliminates the thinking the student was supposed to do

Both rest on a more basic question: what does the student’s working memory actually contain right now? An AI tool that takes a student artifact as input can ask exactly that question. This workshop builds a tool to ask it.

title: Theory: A CLT-Grounded Diagnostic Taxonomy
section: The substrate: classical CLT load types
text:
The substrate: classical CLT load types









Load Type
Source
Effect on Learning
Design Implication




Intrinsic Load
Inherent complexity of the material relative to the learner’s existing schemas
Necessary for learning, but can cause overload
Sequence simple-to-complex; chunk; use worked examples


Extraneous Load
Task or material design that doesn’t serve schema construction
Harmful — does not contribute to learning
Eliminate redundancy; integrate sources; reduce surface complexity


Germane Processing
Effortful schema construction by the learner
Helpful — this is where learning happens
Provide scaffolds that prompt elaboration, not just retrieval



Total cognitive load = intrinsic + extraneous + germane. The teacher’s job is to manage intrinsic load to the learner’s capacity, eliminate extraneous load, and create conditions where germane processing can occur.

The framing of germane load was revised in Sweller, Ayres and Kalyuga (2019) from “germane load” (a third type of load) to “germane processing” (the working-memory work that builds long-term-memory schemas). The diagnostic taxonomy below uses this updated framing.

title: Theory: A CLT-Grounded Diagnostic Taxonomy
text:
The five diagnostic signals
Three of these signals correspond directly to the classical load types. Two more come from schema-acquisition research: a learner can have an absent schema (schema_gap) or an actively wrong one (active_misconception). All five are visible in student artifacts when you know what to look for.

intrinsic_overload
The learner is tracking too many interacting elements at once for their current schemas to handle. The response shows partial reasoning that breaks down, lost threads, mid-explanation derailments.

Example (engineering): a student listing twelve possible causes of a bug and not choosing one.

The mechanism: working memory has been exceeded. The intervention is to chunk the task so element-interactivity falls within capacity (segment_intrinsic_load).


extrinsic_distractor
Cognitive effort is going to the wrong place. The student fixates on irrelevant surface features of the task, the material, or the institutional process around it. The actual learning target is not where attention has landed.

Example (social work): a student analysing a missed-appointment case by checking whether the intake forms are up to date.

The mechanism: extraneous load has captured the limited working-memory budget. The intervention is to declutter the task surface so the substantive question becomes the salient one (reduce_extrinsic_load).


germane_disengagement
The student retrieves correct information but does not elaborate on it. The response is technically right and pedagogically empty: rote knowledge surfacing without contact with the specific case.

Example (statistics): a student reciting the textbook definition of correlation when asked to interpret a specific value.

The mechanism: germane processing is not happening. The student is in retrieval mode, not in schema-construction mode. The intervention is a probe that forces application or self-explanation (prompt_germane_processing).


schema_gap
A foundational concept needed to engage with the task is simply absent. The student often knows something is missing and may say so explicitly.

Example (business): a student asking “is there a formula for whether customers will still buy as many?” — they have correctly identified the missing concept (price elasticity).

The mechanism: the relevant long-term-memory schema does not exist yet. The intervention is to build a bridge from existing schemas to the missing one (activate_prior_schema).


active_misconception
The student is reasoning consistently from a coherent but wrong model. The reasoning is internally self-consistent — that is what makes misconceptions hard to dislodge.

Example (nursing): a student believing high INR means thick blood and confidently increasing the warfarin dose.

The mechanism: a wrong schema is activated and being applied. The intervention is to surface the contrast between the wrong model and the right one, typically through a worked example (replace_misconception).

title: Theory: A CLT-Grounded Diagnostic Taxonomy
text:
Mapping diagnosis to intervention
The shell’s output schema couples each load_signal with a default intervention. The defaults are not the only valid choice; severity and discipline modulate them. But the defaults are a useful baseline.








Diagnosis (load_signal)
Default intervention
What the intervention does




intrinsic_overload
segment_intrinsic_load
Chunks the task so element-interactivity drops below capacity


extrinsic_distractor
reduce_extrinsic_load
Declutters the surface so attention can find the substantive target


germane_disengagement
prompt_germane_processing
Forces application or self-explanation through a probe


schema_gap
activate_prior_schema
Bridges from an existing schema to the missing one via analogy


active_misconception
replace_misconception
Contrasts the wrong model with the right one, often through a worked example

title: Theory: A CLT-Grounded Diagnostic Taxonomy
text:
Why a fixed schema
The shell you will use in the Build block fixes the five diagnostic categories and the five intervention categories. It does not ask you to design them.
The reason is methodological. The categories are the pedagogical decomposition. Every choice the LLM makes when classifying a student response is a CLT-grounded choice. Your work as a tool designer is to teach the model how those categories appear in your discipline. The structure stays put; the discipline-specific cues are what you contribute.

title: Theory: A CLT-Grounded Diagnostic Taxonomy
text:
A meta point about decomposition
This workshop’s tool is itself a worked example. Designing diagnostic AI tools for teaching often gets framed as data-modelling work: “what fields should this return?” That framing turns pedagogical thinking into engineering thinking. By fixing the schema as the CLT taxonomy, the tool removes data-modelling as a degree of freedom and forces the design work to live where it belongs: in noticing what learning looks like in your specific discipline.

title: Theory: A CLT-Grounded Diagnostic Taxonomy
text:
What you do next
You will pick one of six discipline scenarios, each with three calibrated student responses. You will write a system prompt that tells the LLM how to apply the five categories to your discipline. You will test, iterate, and export a portable prompt you can use in any LLM interface.

title: Opening: A Diagnostic Moment
text:
Welcome
Before we get into theory, a moment of recall.

title: Opening: A Diagnostic Moment
text: Think-Pair-Share: a misdiagnosis you remember

title: Opening: A Diagnostic Moment
text:
THINK (3 minutes)
Bring to mind a moment when you misjudged what a student knew or what was going wrong with their thinking. The moment can be from any context: a written assignment, a discussion comment, an exam answer, a question they asked, a comment they made in passing.
Hold the moment for a beat. Try to recall:

What did the student say or write?
What did you initially conclude they did or didn’t understand?
What turned out to be actually happening?

If two moments come to mind, pick the one that was most surprising in retrospect.

title: Opening: A Diagnostic Moment
text:
PAIR (4 minutes)
Tell your neighbour about your moment, and listen to theirs. Then compare:

Were the two moments structurally similar (same kind of mismatch between your initial reading and what was actually happening) or very different?
When you were teaching that student, did you have a clear name or category for what turned out to be going on?

title: Opening: A Diagnostic Moment
text:
SHARE (3 minutes)
A few volunteers share moments. The instructor will note the kinds of mismatches that come up: students with confident-sounding wrong models, students retrieving correct facts without engaging, students stuck on irrelevant features, students missing prerequisites, students juggling too many pieces.
These are exactly the categories we will use today.

title: Opening: A Diagnostic Moment
text:
The bridge to today’s workshop
The diagnostic problem you just remembered is the daily work of teaching: looking at a student artifact and reading what is actually happening in their working memory.
Today’s tool gives an LLM a fixed cognitive-load-theory taxonomy and asks you to teach it how that taxonomy looks in your discipline. The output is a quick, structured read on a student response: what kind of cognitive signal is it, and what intervention fits.

title: Opening: A Diagnostic Moment
text:
The workshop as worked example
This workshop is itself a worked example of CLT-grounded design. The diagnostic categories are fixed by us; your work is in the discipline-specific cues. That decomposition (theory provides structure, practitioner provides domain) is the move we want you to take back to your teaching.

title: Extend: From Tool to Practice
text:
Purpose
You now have a configured tool, a portable prompt, and a calibration record. This block is for stepping back and asking what you actually have, where it serves your teaching, and where it does not.
This is reflection and design thinking, not coding.

title: Extend: From Tool to Practice
text: Question 1: tool versus recipe

title: Extend: From Tool to Practice
text:
Think (3 minutes)
You leave this workshop with two artifacts of different kinds:

The deployed tool: the shell URL with your prompt baked in. Anyone with the link can run diagnostics through your prompt against student responses.
The portable recipe: the exported markdown block. Pastes into any LLM you have institutional access to, including Microsoft Copilot.

When does each one serve you better?









Situation
Tool
Recipe
Why




Quick diagnostic on a single student response in office hours





Routine triage of a class set of short answers





Sharing the diagnostic approach with a colleague





Working without a network connection





Working with sensitive student data that cannot leave the institution

title: Extend: From Tool to Practice
text:
Discuss (4 minutes)
Compare with your neighbour. Where you marked different cells, was the difference about your discipline, your institutional context, or your personal workflow?
The answer “the recipe is always better than the tool” is a perfectly defensible position. So is the opposite. The interesting work is in articulating why one is better for you.

title: Extend: From Tool to Practice
section: Question 2: the load signal that matters most
text: Question 2: the load signal that matters most

title: Extend: From Tool to Practice
text:
Think (3 minutes)
Of the five load_signal categories, which one do you most need to be able to detect reliably in your discipline?
Reasons it might matter most:

It is the most common failure mode among your students
It is the one you are most likely to misdiagnose without help
It is the one whose intervention your teaching currently lacks
It is the one that distinguishes “still learning” from “needs a different approach”

Pick the category and write one sentence on why.

title: Extend: From Tool to Practice
text:
Share (5 minutes)
Volunteers share their pick and reasoning. The instructor will note which categories cluster across the room. The clustering itself is informative: it shows where this audience’s teaching most needs diagnostic help.

title: Extend: From Tool to Practice
text: What you take back

title: Extend: From Tool to Practice
text:
The minimum useful thing
If you do nothing else after this workshop, you have:

A diagnostic vocabulary: five categories that name what is happening in a student response, grounded in cognitive load theory and schema-acquisition research.
A portable prompt: a markdown recipe you can paste into Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT, or Claude on Monday morning, and use on real student work.
A calibration record: knowledge of which signals your prompt distinguishes reliably and which it does not, so you know where to trust the tool and where to second-guess it.

The vocabulary is the point. The tool is the medium.

title: Demo: The Diagnostic Shell in Action
text:
What the instructor will demonstrate

1. The fixed schema (2 minutes)
Open the Output schema (fixed, not editable) accordion below the prompt editor. The five load_signal categories and five intervention categories are visible. These are the cognitive-load-theory taxonomy from the theory section, rendered as data fields. They are not editable: this is the deliberate design choice the workshop turns on.


2. The starter system prompt (3 minutes)
Read through the starter system prompt. Notice three things:

It names each load_signal and gives a generic cue for what it looks like.
It maps each diagnosis to a default intervention.
It is generic on purpose: it works across disciplines but says nothing specific about any one of them. Your work in the Build block will be to localise it.



3. Test on a calibrated response (5 minutes)
Pick the Nursing: Warfarin and INR scenario. Three calibrated student responses are loaded; the instructor will run Response B (the active_misconception: “high INR means thick blood, increase the dose”).
Watch the structured output:

load_signal: should report active_misconception
evidence: should quote or paraphrase the wrong-model line
severity: usually fundamental for an inverted dosing model
intervention: should default to replace_misconception
content: should be specific corrective text

The diagnosis is grounded in the schema. The flexibility is in the prompt and the discipline-specific cues.


4. Edit the prompt, watch behaviour change (3 minutes)
The instructor will add one nursing-specific cue to the system prompt (e.g., “in pharmacology contexts, watch for inverted dose-response models — students sometimes invert the relationship between a lab value and the drug it monitors”). Re-run the same response and observe how the diagnosis becomes more confident or the domain_notes becomes more useful.
This is what you will do in Lab 3, in your own discipline.


5. The export (2 minutes)
Open the Export portable prompt section. The markdown block you see contains your full prompt plus the schema description, ready to paste into Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT, or Claude.ai. The instructor will copy it into a separate Copilot or ChatGPT tab and run it on the same nursing response. Same diagnosis, different tool.

title: Social work: Missed appointments
text: Domain: Social work — case assessment

title: Social work: Missed appointments
text:
Teaching task

A client receiving substance-use counselling has missed three appointments in a row. What would you consider before reaching out, and how would you frame the contact?

title: Social work: Missed appointments
text:
Calibrated student responses

Response A — extrinsic_distractor

First I would check the file to see if any documentation is overdue, and make sure the client’s intake forms are complete in our system. Then I’d verify the contact information is current and check whether their insurance authorization is still active. After that I’d update the case notes to record that contact is pending.


Why this is extrinsic_distractor: the student spends their cognitive effort on agency-process tasks (forms, billing, notes) instead of the substantive question (the client’s wellbeing and engagement). Effort goes to the wrong place.



Response B — active_misconception

Three missed appointments means the client isn’t taking their recovery seriously. I would call them and remind them of their commitments and explain that if they miss another one we may have to close the case. We can’t help people who don’t show up.


Why this is active_misconception: the student reasons coherently from a wrong model (client = autonomous decision-maker who is choosing not to comply). The model needs replacing, not refining: structural and clinical factors are entirely outside the frame.



Response C — intrinsic_overload

There could be many reasons: relapse, transportation, work schedule, mental health, family crisis, housing instability, stigma, fear of judgment, distrust of the agency, transportation costs, childcare, language barriers, immigration status concerns, conflict with previous staff, perceived lack of progress, or just feeling overwhelmed by the process itself.


Why this is intrinsic_overload: the student tracks many real and relevant possibilities but cannot prioritise or move from list to action. The element-interactivity exceeds working-memory capacity, so analysis collapses into enumeration.

Why calibrated responses
The calibration is a teaching device, not a claim that a response can only mean one thing. Real student responses are messy and often blend signals. The calibrated responses are constructed to lean strongly toward one load_signal so that you can:

Test whether your prompt distinguishes that signal from the others
Iterate when it does not
Notice the cases where two signals genuinely co-occur (those will be your discipline’s hardest diagnostic edges)


The scenario you pick determines which three of the five load_signal categories you will exercise. The combinations are deliberate: each scenario covers categories that are particularly distinguishable in that discipline’s idiom.

title: Education: Critique a quiz question
text: Domain: Education / pedagogy — assessment design

title: Education: Critique a quiz question
text:
Teaching task

Critique this multiple-choice item and suggest improvements: “The capital of Switzerland is: a) Zurich b) Geneva c) Bern d) All of the above”

title: Education: Critique a quiz question
text:
Calibrated student responses

Response A — germane_disengagement

Multiple choice questions should have a clear stem, plausible distractors, only one correct answer, and avoid ‘all of the above’ or ‘none of the above’ as options. They should test higher-order thinking when possible. The distractors should be roughly the same length.


Why this is germane_disengagement: the student recites generic MC-design rules accurately, but never engages with the specific item in front of them. They retrieve a checklist instead of analysing the example.



Response B — extrinsic_distractor

The question is problematic because Bern is also the name of a canton, and students might confuse the city of Bern with the canton of Bern. So you’d need to specify ‘city’ or ‘capital city’ clearly. Also, the German spelling can be ambiguous between cantons and cities.


Why this is extrinsic_distractor: the student fixates on a tangential surface feature (Bern as canton vs. city) rather than the substantive design problem (the broken “all of the above” option in a question with one correct factual answer).



Response C — active_misconception

I think ‘all of the above’ is fine here because students should know exact facts, and if they pick it that means they don’t know the answer. The question is testing whether they really know the capital, so the trick distractors are useful for catching guessers.


Why this is active_misconception: the student is reasoning consistently from a wrong model of assessment (purpose = catching guessers; trickier = better). The reasoning is coherent within that model, which is exactly why it needs replacing rather than repairing.

Instructions

title: Business: Bakery pricing
text: Domain: Business / economics — pricing strategy

title: Business: Bakery pricing
text:
Teaching task

A small bakery sells bread at CHF 5 per loaf and sells 100 loaves a day. They are considering raising the price to CHF 6. Should they? Justify your answer.

title: Business: Bakery pricing
text:
Calibrated student responses

Response A — active_misconception

Yes, they should raise the price. At CHF 5 they make CHF 500 a day, at CHF 6 they make CHF 600 a day, so they make CHF 100 more per day. That’s CHF 36,500 more per year. It’s better revenue.


Why this is active_misconception: the student applies linear arithmetic confidently and never questions whether quantity sold stays constant when price changes. They have a coherent (but wrong) model: price up = revenue up, period.



Response B — germane_disengagement

It depends on a lot of factors. Like the cost of ingredients, what competitors are charging, how loyal the customers are, whether the bakery has unique products, the location, the demographic of the neighborhood, seasonal variation in demand, the weather, what time of year it is, marketing budget, and the bakery’s brand. You’d need to consider all of these.


Why this is germane_disengagement: the student lists many real factors but does no actual analysis. Retrieval-without-elaboration: they have produced a checklist instead of applying the core concept (price elasticity of demand).



Response C — schema_gap

I’m not sure how to think about this. If they raise the price they get more money per loaf but I don’t know how to figure out if customers will still buy as many. Is there a formula?


Why this is schema_gap: the student correctly identifies what they don’t know (how to model demand response) and explicitly asks for the missing concept (price elasticity). The prerequisite schema is simply absent.

title: Engineering: Stale-data bug
text: Domain: Technical / engineering — software diagnosis

title: Engineering: Stale-data bug
text:
Teaching task

A web form sometimes shows old data after a user submits an update. The bug only happens for some users. Where would you start investigating, and why?

title: Engineering: Stale-data bug
text:
Calibrated student responses

Response A — active_misconception

It’s a database issue. The database is not being updated when the form is submitted. I would look at the database write logic in the code and find where the SQL UPDATE statement is failing. The data is clearly not being saved.


Why this is active_misconception: the student commits to one cause (database write failure) on the basis of a coherent but wrong model. They ignore the “sometimes” and “some users” clues that point at caching, session, or CDN layers.



Response B — schema_gap

I’d check the HTML form to make sure all the fields have the right names, and verify the CSS isn’t hiding anything. Maybe the form isn’t displaying the new data correctly because of a styling issue or the form fields aren’t connected properly to the submit button.


Why this is schema_gap: the student reasons from front-end-only concepts (HTML, CSS, form fields) and never reaches for the relevant prerequisite concept (caching, request-response state, server-side data flow). The schema needed for this kind of bug is not present.



Response C — intrinsic_overload

The bug could be caused by: browser caching, CDN caching, server-side caching, session-state desync, replica lag in the database, an outdated build deployed to some servers, race conditions in the request handler, eventual consistency in distributed storage, a stale local-storage value, a service worker serving cached responses, missing cache-control headers, A/B test bucket assignment, or a load balancer routing some users to an older server version. I would investigate all of these.


Why this is intrinsic_overload: the student names many real and plausible causes but cannot strategise. The interactivity between possibilities exceeds working-memory and the response stops at enumeration rather than producing a triage plan.

title: Nursing: Warfarin and INR
text: Domain: Health sciences / nursing — pharmacology

title: Nursing: Warfarin and INR
text:
Teaching task

A patient on long-term warfarin presents at the clinic with an INR of 5.2. Explain what you would do next and why.

title: Nursing: Warfarin and INR
text:
Calibrated student responses

Response A — intrinsic_overload

I would check the patient’s vitamin K intake recently and also their last dose of warfarin and look at their kidney and liver function and ask about any new medications they started because that all affects INR… so I would check the dosing schedule too and probably reduce the dose or hold it, depending on bleeding risk, but it’s also important to see if they have any signs of bleeding because that changes the urgency, and we’d also need to consider if vitamin K should be given but only if the INR is really high or there’s bleeding so I think we’d hold the dose first and recheck.


Why this is intrinsic_overload: the student is tracking many interacting elements (vitamin K, dosing, comorbidities, bleeding risk, drug interactions) at once. Each element is correct on its own, but the response loses its thread and never lands on a clear plan.



Response B — active_misconception

Since the INR is high at 5.2, I would increase the warfarin dose so the patient’s blood doesn’t clot too much. INR shows how thick the blood is, and high INR means the blood is too thick.


Why this is active_misconception: the student has a coherent but inverted mental model — they believe high INR means thick blood. The reasoning is internally consistent, the wrong schema is being applied confidently.



Response C — schema_gap

I would tell the doctor and ask what they want me to do. I’m not sure what 5.2 means: is that high or normal? What’s the normal range supposed to be?


Why this is schema_gap: the student lacks the prerequisite concept (the therapeutic INR range for warfarin patients). They are not confused or overloaded; the relevant prior knowledge is simply absent.

title: Statistics: Interpreting r = 0.3
text: Domain: Statistics / research methods — interpreting effects

title: Statistics: Interpreting r = 0.3
text:
Teaching task

A study reports a correlation of \(r = 0.3\) between hours studied per week and end-of-semester exam grade. How would you interpret this for a colleague who hasn’t seen the data?

title: Statistics: Interpreting r = 0.3
text:
Calibrated student responses

Response A — active_misconception

This shows that studying causes higher grades. The more hours you study, the better your grade will be. So we should tell students to study more if they want to do better on exams.


Why this is active_misconception: the student reasons confidently from a wrong model (correlation = causation) and produces an actionable but inappropriate conclusion. The model needs replacing.



Response B — germane_disengagement

Correlation is a measure of the linear relationship between two variables, ranging from \(-1\) to \(+1\). A value of \(0\) means no relationship, \(+1\) means perfect positive relationship, \(-1\) means perfect negative relationship. So \(r = 0.3\) means there is a positive correlation between the two variables.


Why this is germane_disengagement: the student recites the textbook definition correctly but never applies it to interpret the specific value. They retrieve without elaborating on what \(r = 0.3\) actually means in this context.



Response C — schema_gap

I’m not sure how to interpret \(0.3\). Is that a strong correlation or a weak one? I know that \(1.0\) would be perfect but I don’t have a sense of what counts as meaningful in between.


Why this is schema_gap: the student honestly identifies the missing piece (a sense of effect-size magnitude in their field). The prerequisite calibration is not yet in place; this is a gap, not a misconception.

title: Closing: One Commitment
section: Pedagogy provides structure; practitioners provide cues
text:
Pedagogy provides structure; practitioners provide cues
The decomposition this workshop turned on was:

Theory provides structure. The five load_signal categories were not invented for this tool; they were derived from CLT and schema-acquisition research. They are the same five whatever discipline you teach.
Practitioners provide cues. What an intrinsic_overload looks like in nursing differs from what it looks like in business or social work. Your discipline expertise is what makes the structure usable.

This is the move we want you to take back to your teaching with AI. When you reach for a new AI tool, ask: where is the theory in this, and where is the discipline expertise? If the answer is “neither,” the tool is doing something other than supporting learning.

title: Closing: One Commitment
text:

If you want to see a more elaborated example of CLT-grounded tool design, the Worked Example Weaver is a sister tool that generates personalized worked examples across three domains. It is a deliberately heavier piece of software than today’s diagnostic shell, and serves as a reference for what a fuller tool with a more complex structure looks like.

title: Closing: One Commitment
text:
Frequently asked questions

Q: What if my discipline does not fit any of the five categories?
This is the most common pushback and worth taking seriously. Two responses:
First, the categories are deliberately broad. intrinsic_overload is not “exam stress” but “too much element-interactivity for current schemas” — that shows up in every discipline, including yours.
Second, if a response genuinely falls outside the categories, that is information. The tool will produce a low-confidence diagnosis, the domain_notes field will surface what the categories missed, and you have a research finding: in your discipline, here is a load signal not captured by the standard taxonomy. That is interesting and worth keeping.
Q: How do I trust the LLM’s diagnosis?
You don’t, fully. The tool is a triage aid, not an oracle. Workshop Lab 4’s calibration test exists exactly to map where your prompt produces reliable diagnoses and where it does not. Use the tool where it is reliable; second-guess it where it is not. Note that the same caution applies to your own diagnostic intuitions, which is partly the workshop’s point.
Q: What about students using Copilot themselves on the same artifact?
Different question. The tool you built is a teacher’s diagnostic aid: it reads student work for the cognitive signal. A student running their own work through Copilot for feedback is doing something different (and often something we worry about). The intermediate workshop’s offloading-vs-outsourcing framing applies here.
Q: Will this scale to a class of 200?
Yes, with caveats. The portable prompt runs on whatever institutional LLM you have access to, and the per-call cost is small. The cap is your time spent reviewing the diagnoses. A reasonable workflow is to use the tool for first-pass triage and then deeply read the responses the tool flags as severity: fundamental.

text:

You came in expecting to develop something. You did: a diagnostic vocabulary, a working tool, and a recipe. None of it required code. All of it was pedagogical thinking made operational.

Workshop Structure: An Applied Worked Example






ImportantThis Workshop IS a Worked Example



This workshop demonstrates the principle it teaches by being structured as a worked example of CLT-grounded design.
Traditional approach (problem-solving):

Define your tool’s data structures, design the schema, implement the LLM call, build a UI, deploy.

This is too much for a 3-hour workshop and not what most participants need to know.
This approach (worked example):

The structure is given. The intelligence lives in the prompt. Your work is making the structure speak your discipline’s language.

Why? The decomposition (theory provides structure, practitioner provides cues) is the move we want participants to take back to their teaching with AI. Doing it once at workshop scale lets participants feel the leverage.
